lessons.title: Money matters

image.describe: a small brown leather purse open on a wooden table with money inside

items.note: Say ‘coins’ for small round metal money.

image.describe: a small pile of shiny gold and silver metal coins on a table

items.note: Use ‘notes’ for paper money.

items.example: Here is your change.
items.note: ‘Change’ is the money a shop gives back when you pay more than the cost, or small coins.

items.example: I cannot afford that expensive coat.
items.note: Say ‘can afford’ when you have enough money to buy something.

items.example: I get pocket money every weekend.
items.note: ‘Pocket money’ is a small amount of money parents give children each week.

grammar.title: can afford / cannot afford
grammar.explanation: Use can afford when you have enough money to buy something, and cannot afford when something is too expensive for you.
examples: We cannot afford a new car.

mission.setup: Smarty asks you about your money before shopping in the market square. Answer in your own words.

turns.smarty: I have three notes in my purse. Do you have notes or coins?

turns.smarty: Do you get pocket money every week?

turns.hint: Answer Yes or No, or say when you get pocket money.

lessons.title: Bargains
lessons.scenario: Smarty and Sam look for good deals in the market square.

items.example: These blue shoes are on sale today.
items.note: Say ‘on sale’ when a shop sells something for less money than usual.

items.example: Ten notes for a warm coat is a good deal.
items.note: Call something ‘a good deal’ when you pay very little for what you get.

items.example: Students get a twenty percent discount here.
items.note: A ‘discount’ is money taken off the usual cost.

items.example: There is a special offer on fruit this morning.
items.note: A ‘special offer’ is a short-time deal to help people buy more.

items.example: Sorry, the red T-shirt is out of stock.
items.note: Say ‘out of stock’ when a shop has sold all of an item and has none left.

items.example: Socks are buy one get one free at that shop.
items.note: ‘Buy one get one free’ means you pay for one item and get a second one for zero money.

grammar.title: Zero conditional for shopping facts
grammar.explanation: Use if + present simple, present simple to talk about shopping rules and things that are always true.
examples: If a shirt is on sale, you get a discount.
If something is out of stock, you cannot buy it now.

lessons.title: Returns
lessons.scenario: Ben brings faulty headphones back to a shop in the market square.

items.example: Always keep your receipt after you pay.
items.note: A ‘receipt’ is the piece of paper showing what you bought and paid.

items.example: Can I have a refund, please?
items.note: A ‘refund’ is when a shop gives your money back.

items.example: I would like to exchange this shirt for a bigger size.
items.note: To ‘exchange’ means to swap one item for another in the shop.

items.example: This lamp is faulty because it does not turn on.
items.note: Say ‘faulty’ when a new thing is broken or does not work properly.

items.example: I would like to return these headphones.
items.note: Say ‘I would like to return…’ to politely bring something back to a shop.

items.example: You can return any shirt within thirty days.
items.note: ‘Within thirty days’ means before thirty days have passed.

practice.prompt: What paper do you need to show when you bring something back to a shop?

lessons.title: Saving
lessons.scenario: Smarty helps Tom and Lily plan how to save up for a new bicycle.

items.example: I am saving up for a new bicycle.
items.note: Say ‘save up’ when you keep money over time to buy something big later.

items.example: Do not spend all your pocket money in one day.
items.note: ‘Spend’ means to use money to pay for things.

items.example: If you buy broken toys, you waste your money.
items.note: ‘Waste’ means to spend money badly on things you do not need.

items.example: Smart people invest money in good books and tools.
items.note: ‘Invest’ means to put money or time into something that grows or helps you later.

items.example: Can you lend me two coins for the bus?
items.note: ‘Lend’ means to give someone money for a short time until they give it back.

items.example: I owe Sam five notes from yesterday.
items.note: ‘Owe’ means you must pay money back to someone who lent it to you.

grammar.title: First conditional for future money plans
grammar.explanation: Use if + present simple, will + verb to talk about real future results of your money choices.
examples: If you save up every week, you will afford a new bicycle.
If you waste all your money, you will not have any for later.

practice.prompt: Tom wants a new laptop, so he keeps his pocket money in a box every week. What is he doing?
practice.explanation: Saving up means keeping money over time for something special.

options: You lent me ten notes, so I owe you ten notes.
You spent ten notes, so I owe you ten notes.
You wasted ten notes, so I owe you ten notes.
practice.explanation: When someone lends you money, you owe that money to them.

practice.prompt: Match the money verbs with their meanings.

pairs.right: spend money when you do not need to
keep money so you get more

practice.explanation: Spending, wasting, and investing are three different ways to use money.

grammar.title: Quantifiers: too much, enough, plenty of, hardly any
